newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plains flood dikes hold, focus turns north.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plains flood dikes hold, focus turns north.

text.p: The overflowing Red River crested in Fargo Saturday, and officials said the dikes and sandbags holding back the floodwaters were largely intact as the focus moved north toward Grand Forks.

Capt. Patrick Richards of North Dakota's Emergency Management division said nearly 290 Army and Air National Guards were on duty sandbagging, working on the dikes and providing emergency generators for power, among other things.
"We've got all kinds of missions going on," he said. "There is still a lot of local diking operations and containment operations in the Fargo-Moorhead area."
He said residents north of Fargo continued to prepare for the river's onslaught.
"Grand Forks seems to be very well prepared, but they're not letting their guard down," he said. "They continue to work individual levels as well as shoring up some of the major containment systems."

The National Weather Service forecast the Red River to crest at East Grand Forks, Minnesota, which is about 65 miles (40 km) north of Fargo and across the river from Grand Forks, N.D., at 49 feet (15 meters) sometime during the week of April 21.
It said the river was currently at 42 feet (12.8 meters), 14 feet (4.3 meters) above flood stage at East Grand Forks.

In Fargo, the river, which forms the border of North Dakota and Minnesota, had crested at about 37.6 feet (11.5 meters), and only minor fluctuations were expected, officials said. Flood stage is at 17 feet (5.2 meters).
But as temperatures warmed above freezing, melting snow raised concern about another possible crest as water levels remained at historically high levels.
"We're still concerned a little bit about runoff. There's still a tremendous amount of water against the sandbags," said Dennis Walaker, director of operations at the Fargo engineering department.
"All clay dikes are in good condition," Walaker said. "We continue to have isolated problems with sandbag dikes and private homes."
He said the city had three truckloads full of sandbags ready to be sent out to plug leaks.
Officials said the river level was slowly beginning to drop, particularly in the southern part of Fargo, but the threat of a second crest and more flooding remained.
"We still have a lot of snow out there and as the temperatures continue to rise now through next week, that's going to melt and we're going to have a lot of overland water," Richards said.
"We have a lot of nervous people out there and they will be for probably another five or six days," Walaker said.
